title: If you miss the straightforward action RPGs of the past, try the generous demo for Darkstone Restoration
author: Jody Macgregor
content:
Before action RPGs relied on seasonal ladders and DLC treadmills there was Darkstone, a 1999 hack and slash where you clicked on things until they died and liked it. It had some interesting ideas, like the companion mode that lets you switch between two player-characters, the other controlled by the CPU while you took the lead, but it remained true to the basics of a genre I got into precisely because it was basic.

Now it's back, with a remaster in early access that improves the UI and controls (you can move characters with WASD now, or play with a controller), and the graphics (though I had to turn off volumetric fog and procedural grass for the sake of my poor framerate).

It's got a demo too, which lets you make characters from any of its eight classes and explore the early-game dungeons, letting you play three of its quests, which are selected at random each time you start a new game.

It's just nice to start up an action RPG without having to worry about which build I'm going to pursue, or look at a massive node full of future skill unlocks, or wonder if I should start a seasonal character or whether I'm missing out by not buying the latest DLC. Darkstone is just Darkstone, a game of clicking on skeletons and goblins until they die, and as that annoying guy who though the first Diablo was the best Diablo it's really scratching the itch.

I want an action RPG that understands these are games I play when I need a break from thinky puzzly heavy games and want something light and, you know, more action-packed. I'll get back into them later, right now I really want to fight some giant wasps in a hole in the ground. Darkstone Restoration is perfect for that.

The only notable thing missing from the early access build is online multiplayer, though it does have couch co-op. A permadeath mode is also in the works. You can download the demo on Steam.

Jody's first computer was a Commodore 64, so he remembers having to use a code wheel to play Pool of Radiance. A former music journalist who interviewed everyone from Giorgio Moroder to Trent Reznor, Jody also co-hosted Australia's first radio show about videogames, Zed Games. title: Second Lawsuit Challenging Trump's New Section 301 Tariffs Filed
author: IlyaSomin
content:
Donald Trump

Second Lawsuit Challenging Trump's New Section 301 Tariffs Filed

It was filed by several businesses, including Learning Resources, Inc., which was also involved in the IEEPA tariff litigation.

| 7.24.2026 10:08 PM

In my last post, I did a brief overview of the new lawsuit challenging Trump's massive new Section 301 lawsuits filed by the Liberty Justice Center on behalf of two small businesses. LJC is the public interest law firm  I worked with on V.O.S. Selections v. Trump, the IEEPA tariff case decided by the Supreme Court in February. There is now a second lawsuit challenging the tariffs, Learning Resources, Inc. v. United States. Their complaint is available here.

This case was filed by a group of several businesses, with  Learning Resources, Inc., as the lead plaintiff. Learning Resources, which is a toy manufacturer, is the same firm whose case was consolidated with ours in the IEEPA litigation, and eventually gave its name to the Supreme Court decision. In that instance, their case was dismissed on jurisdictional grounds (it was, the justices decided, filed in the wrong court) and ours prevailed. In the present case, everyone agrees the only possible venue is the US Court of International Trade (CIT), where we filed our IEEPA case, and which also recently ruled against Trump's Section 122 tariffs (in another case brought by LJC). Trump's tariffs are making the CIT's workload great again!

As in the IEEPA litigation, Learning Resources is represented by prominent appellate litigator Pratik Shah, and others at Akin Gump.

The issues raised in the Learning Resources complaint are very similar to those in the LJC case. They too argue that the Section 301 tariffs violate statutory requirements, and that if Section 301 did grant the president the power to impose these massive tariffs, it would violate the constitutional nondelegation doctrine. But, unlike the LJC complaint, this one does not invoke the major questions doctrine. It also does not seek a class action certification. Thus, relief granted by the court would likely be limited to the specific plaintiff firms.

I think it likely that CIT will consolidate these two cases and consider them together. There may well be more Section 301 cases filed by businesses, public interest groups, and possibly state governments. We shall see.

title: US appeals court continues ban on $100K fee for H-1B visas
content:
US appeals court continues ban on $100K fee for H-1B visas

The US Court of Appeals for the First District on Friday denied the Trump administration’s appeal of a US District Court ruling that blocked the president’s proclamation of a new $100,000 fee for H-1B visas. The three-judge panel found that the administration was unlikely to succeed on appeal.

H-1B visas are employer-sponsored non-immigrant visas issued to foreign workers with specialized knowledge and a bachelor’s degree or higher. Technology companies are the biggest users of H-1B visas, which are valid for three years with a possible three-year extension. Congress caps the program at 65,000 visas per year, with an additional 20,000 allowed for workers with advanced degrees. Before the proclamation, employers typically paid about $2000 to $5000 to obtain the visas.

Twenty states, led by California, sued the administration to block the fee created by President Donald Trump’s administration. In his proclamation, Trump said that employers have abused the program, hiring foreign workers for less money while cutting wages and jobs for Americans.

Judge Leo Sorkin, US District Court for the District of Massachusetts, held in favor of the states. He ruled that the new fee is a tax. The separation of powers in the US Constitution gives only Congress the authority to levy taxes and to determine immigration policy. The fee also violated the Administrative Procedure Act.

The US Chamber of Commerce has also sued to block the $100,000 fee, calling it unfair to start-ups and small to midsize businesses that often need expert workers from overseas to grow. The US District Court for the District of Columbia upheld the fee in December 2025. The Chamber of Commerce appealed, and the case is still pending.

title: UN experts decry resumed US-Iran strikes
content:
News

UN experts decry resumed US-Iran strikes

UN experts on Thursday decried the continuation of hostilities between the US and Iran, warning that the resumed conflict undermines peace and greatly increases civilian suffering in the region. Human rights authorities condemned the strikes and counter-strikes and emphasized the impact on civilians. Strikes on vessels operating within the Strait of Hormuz are “endangering civilian seafarers, and freedom of navigation,” the experts warned.

The UN also highlighted that US strikes on Iranian infrastructure hit a desalination plant, caused power outages, and inflicted damage on railways. There have also been reports of attacks on the Semnan Airport, a wheat silo, a bottled water factory, and “areas adjacent to a children’s cancer hospital in Ahvaz.” Iran’s Ministry of Health reported 50 dead and more than 500 injured.

The UN experts said that civilians—especially the most vulnerable of society, including children, women, refugees, persons with disabilities, and people living in poverty—are paying high costs:

The people of Iran are once again caught between renewed US strikes and their government’s internal repression… Those losing their lives include fishermen, night-shift workers caught in the strikes, and residents of informal settlements… Strikes on ports, power supplies and transport links sever communities from food, medicine and livelihoods in a country in deep economic precarity and have serious climate change implications.

On June 14, the White House announced that it reached a tentative peace deal with Iran. The Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Iran contained 14 key points, including the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz within 30 days of signing, lifting US sanctions on Iran, and instituting a ceasefire while the deal is finalized within a maximum timeframe of 60 days, “extendable with mutual consent.”

However, the ceasefire collapsed after Iran carried out strikes on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. The US has since begun a series of retaliatory strikes, which have increased in intensity and resulted in many casualties and significant infrastructure damage.

The Geneva Conventions of 1949 state that civilians must remain protected during armed conflict, and Article 52 of Additional Protocol I outlines protections for “civilian objects,” including infrastructure. While the US is bound by the Geneva Conventions, it has not ratified Additional Protocol I. However, the US has accepted, through the Department of Defense Law of War Manual, that core principles such as distinction, proportionality, and precautions are part of customary international law.

The UN experts strongly urged parties to “de-escalate and return to negotiations” and reminded parties of their obligations under international law.

title: Kingdom Come Salvation could be Warhorse's next medieval history RPG, if this EU trademark filing turns out to be the genuine article
author: Mark Warren
content:
Is this Kingdom Coming next?

Kingdom Come Deliverance developers Warhorse confirmed back in May that they've got a "new Kingdom Come adventure" in the works, alongside a Lord of the Rings RPG. The name of the former looks like it may now have been revealed via a freshly filed EU trademark for the phrase 'Kingdom Come Salvation'.

Originally spotted by Australian site Phrasemaker, this trademark for Kingdom Come Salvation was field yesterday, July 23rd, with the European Union's Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO). The listing features a graphic with the name in the font Warhorse typically use for the names of their Kingdom Come games. It also cites "computer gaming software" and "entertainment services for matching users with computer games" in its 'goods and services' section, suggesting that's what the trademark will be used for.

While the Warhorse Studios profile listed as having filed to own the trademark only has this one application linked to it on the EUIPO site - if it'd also applied for a Kingdom Come Deliverance 2 trademark, that'd have been a bit of a smoking gun - the lawyer listed as having filed for the trademark on their behalf does have a bunch of other trademark applications to her name.

Going by her firm's website, this lawyer named Dana Lukajová is a specialist patent attorney based in the Czech city of Prague, where Warhorse are also based.

I've reached out to Warhorse for comment.

As for what Kingdom Come Salvation'll look like, assuming it is the name of this next entry in the series, the filing offers no more clues. The pivot away from numbered Deliverance sequels could indicate a shift away from telling Henry of Skalitz's story or having him stay on as the protagonist. As TheGamer point out, Central Europe was rocked by the Hussite Wars starting in 1419, not too long after KCD2's adventure in 1403. This series of civil wars revolved around a schism between the established Catholic faith and the followers of proto-protestant Christian reformer Jan Hus, who was executed by the Catholic church in 1415 for heresy.

Naturally, amid all the fighting was plenty of chatter about what concepts like salvation mean or should look like in the context of worship.

title: Blasphemous and Sekiro enjoyers may savour the boss rushing of Rubinite, a dark fantasy action RPG about a red-eyed murder princess
author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
content:
Now that's a knife

If I've learned anything from years of dark fantasy, it's that there's no force in this universe more terrible than a puny-looking girl with a kitchen knife. Just ask Katana Man, or the Queen of Hearts. Or the lolloping wolfbeast I've recently disembowelled in Rubinite, a pretty slick and engrossingly evil boss rush action game from Gameworks Ventures and Cup Dog Games, which is on sale today.

In Rubinite, you play Ruby, outcast princess of a Scarlet Kingdom that has been conquered by a sorceress who really enjoys plucking out people's eyes. To defeat the sorceress, Ruby must first annihilate a menagerie of sentinels that range from an overclocked caterpillar to a swordswoman in the approximate vein of Elden Ring's Malenia.

Ruby's knife inflicts minimal damage by itself, but usefully, she has the ability to identify and mark each enemy's weak points by holding a controller trigger and aiming with analog stick to fill a bar. She can do this up to three times, before performing a devastating attack. The catch is that she can't move while marking weak points, though she can dodge with exact timing during the process to immediately fill up the bar. If she takes damage, any marked weakpoints will be dispelled.

While not without precedent – see Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice's deathblows system – it's a refreshing break from the attritional exchanges you get in a lot of bossfights. There is no block button to cower behind, so you'll need to memorise the animation timing. It's also not as simplistic as it may sound: you'll level up and acquire talismans that stun opponents or convert chip damage into health potions, among other customisation options. Each boss also adds wrinkles, such as projectiles you can bounce back to sender.

I'm basing this on an hour or so with the demo, mind, so please freely upend your salt shaker over these foolishly confident assertions about the combat's evolution. One thing I can say for sure is that I like Rubinite's world. It serves up lip-smacking pixelgore and august architecture with alarming outbreaks of whimsy. It reminds me a fair bit of Blasphemous.

Between bossfights, you'll return to a shattered tower to level up and bandy words with a handful of NPCs. There's a lizard blacksmith for comic relief, and a lean warrior with an owl-faced helmet. Early on, Owl Face asks you to take soup to a hooded figure tied to a cross in the gaol. The hooded figure begs you to kill him. Are we actually the baddies, Owl Face? The hub area expands as you butcher bosses, with treasures to recover from side rooms.

Again, it's on sale now via Steam. If you need a little more dungeoneering with your boss battering, Death's Door is a fine substitute.

title: The Real Life Mermaids of Florida’s Weeki Wachee Springs
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
There’s been plenty of coverage on the Weeki Wachee mermaids in recent years, and Jack Burke isn’t trying to break any new ground here. But he does manage to bring to life the weird underground theatre where the mermaids have danced for decades, beautifully evoking the wonder of celestial blue light and sparkly tails. Burke’s piece is a gentle homage to “this weird little relic from another age”—a time in America that belonged to the hustlers and the dreamers.

I eventually find a seat in the auditorium, just as a video of Mr Margaritaville himself, Jimmy Buffett, crackles onto the wall-mounted televisions. He launches into a rendition of Fins, featuring a quartet of smiling and costumed Weeki Wachee mermaids being wheeled on stage to backing-dance from their seats. Around me are grandparents in visors, sunburnt dads in fishing shirts, and little girls in glittering mermaid tails clutching plush dolphins.

The lights dim and a syrupy-voiced MC asks us if we’re ready for the mermaids. Inevitably, we are not quite ready enough, and are encouraged to express our excitement a little more vocally.

The dusty blue satin curtain slowly winches itself open, to reveal a thick wall of glass, behind which lies the famous spring itself. A water so clear and turquoise it hardly looks like water at all. Schools of tiny fish drift lazily across the scene. A turtle paddles past with supreme indifference.

And then, rising out of some deeper part of the spring, comes a mermaid.

title: Isolated, Scared, Forlorn: The Heartbreaking Final Months of Virginia Giuffre’s Life
author: Seyward Darby
content:
Virginia Giuffre made global headlines for her fight against her sexual abusers among the wealthy elite, all detailed in a bestselling memoir. Now new questions have emerged about the private anguish the most famous accuser of Jeffrey Epstein faced at home. Her husband, whom she once credited with helping her escape Epstein, had assaulted and tormented her for years:

On March 4, 2015, police attended the Giuffre home after receiving several 911 hang-up calls. According to the police report, Virginia said she tried to stop Robbie punching and kicking their dog, Bear, which Robbie said had bitten him. She said Robbie then punched her several times in her face and head, grabbed her by the throat, and strangled her. Virginia had a bruise forming on her left cheek, blood on her sleeve, and a whitish-clear fluid mixed with blood leaking from her ear, which police noted could be cerebral spinal fluid, a symptom of severe head trauma. Robbie was arrested on domestic violence charges and taken to jail, where he told an officer he’d hit Virginia by accident.

Dale King, the then-detective sergeant who went to check on Virginia the next morning… [says] he remembers Robbie flagged him down in the street. He knew the couple because he’d been to the house to keep the paparazzi in line and investigate the strange break-ins. King said Robbie seemed to be soothing himself with a story he’d heard him narrate before, about being the savior. “He’s trying to convince me that I have to let him get back home so he can protect her,” he says. “Hell,” he remembers thinking. “You’re her biggest threat right now.”

title: A Strange Continent
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
Ben Markovits, an Austin-raised writer long settled in London, returns home with his teenage son and a pair of folding bikes for a ride through the Hill Country. As they pedal from Pedernales Falls toward Salt Lick BBQ, the shifting Texas landscape prompts reflections on English density versus Texan sprawl and on the deeper divide between the two cultures. By journey’s end, Markovits is left reckoning with how places—and our idea of “home”—keep changing, even as we try to return to them, a question that lingers long after the ride is over.

I had hoped, while my kids were still kids, that we’d live in Texas for a year, that they’d know something of my childhood—not just America generally, but something about the neighborhood I grew up in and the space and the year-round warm weather that makes childhood an outdoor sport, and not an indoor one as it is in England from October onward. But it didn’t happen. My daughter is now at university, and my son, 16, is caught up in the two-year cycles of English high school exams. This means the window where this move is still possible for us has closed—except for the one week over Christmas when we fly to Austin and my kids can pretend, in the company of their American cousins, to be Texans.

title: Beckett the Prophet
author: Brendan Fitzgerald
content:
The peg for Robert Zaretsky’s essay on Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot feels flimsy: “the 70th anniversary of its American premiere,” which lagged the show’s proper premiere, in Paris, by three years. Disregard the peg; as Zaretsky makes clear, there’s not a bad time, these days, to consider Beckett’s best-known work, a demonstration of “solidarity and compassion” set against a “featureless, colorless vista.” The stage directions for Godot have Estragon, one of the play’s leads, look out into the auditorium as an extension of the devastation. “Inspiring prospects,” he says. Let’s hope so.

Of course, Godot never arrives. In a Sesame Street parody of the play, the tree, fed up with the melodramatic and nonsensical patter of two Muppets waiting for Elmo, uproots itself and walks off the stage. But we cannot uproot ourselves and walk off the stage; instead, stuck like Didi and Gogo in a state of non-arrival, we wait. For those who waited for an answer from Beckett, none ever came. He once snapped at the English actor Ralph Richardson, who asked if Godot stood for God. If he had meant God, Beckett said, he would have written God. The play, he insisted, strove to avoid definition. This strategy of avoidance leaves us to gaze at a landscape void of meaning, one that by turns is the source of our bemusement and amusement.
